claim: HCT116 colon cancer cell line contains a CD44highEpCAMlow (EpCAMlo) subpopulation representing 5.0% ± 2.5% of cells.
source: Variable percentages of EpCAMlo cells were found to feature the HCT116 (5.0% ± 2.5%) and SW480 (16.7% ± 13%) cell lines, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: SW480 colon cancer cell line contains a CD44highEpCAMlow (EpCAMlo) subpopulation representing 16.7% ± 13% of cells.
source: Variable percentages of EpCAMlo cells were found to feature the HCT116 (5.0% ± 2.5%) and SW480 (16.7% ± 13%) cell lines, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 1A and stated in the text.

claim: EpCAMlo cells have a spindle-shaped and mesenchymal-like morphology.
source: While EpCAMhi cells formed compact colonies with characteristic epithelial morphology, EpCAMlo cells showed a more spindle- and mesenchymal-like appearance.
evidence: The claim is supported by phase-contrast microscopy images shown in Figure 1B.

claim: EpCAMhi cells have a compact epithelial morphology.
source: While EpCAMhi cells formed compact colonies with characteristic epithelial morphology, EpCAMlo cells showed a more spindle- and mesenchymal-like appearance.
evidence: The claim is supported by phase-contrast microscopy images shown in Figure 1B.

claim: EpCAMlo cells from HCT116 produce significantly more liver metastases than EpCAMhi and bulk cells after intrasplenic injection.
source: EpCAMlo cells from both lines resulted in significantly more liver metastases than with EpCAMhi and bulk cells (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1C and images in Figure 1D from intrasplenic injection experiments.

claim: EpCAMlo cells from SW480 produce significantly more liver metastases than EpCAMhi and bulk cells after intrasplenic injection.
source: EpCAMlo cells from both lines resulted in significantly more liver metastases than with EpCAMhi and bulk cells (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1C and images in Figure 1D from intrasplenic injection experiments.

claim: EpCAMlo-derived liver metastases contain predominantly EpCAMhi cells (>99%).
source: FACS analysis of the EpCAMlo-derived liver metastases revealed predominant epithelial features with a vast majority of EpCAMhi cells (>99%), thus highlighting their striking plasticity and the key role played by MET in metastasis formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 5B and Figure 1—source data 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5B.

claim: EpCAMlo cells have significantly increased migratory capacity compared to EpCAMhi cells.
source: Likewise, EpCAMlo cells were shown to have significantly increased migratory and invasive ability when compared with their EpCAMhi counterparts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: EpCAMlo cells have significantly increased invasive capacity compared to EpCAMhi cells.
source: Likewise, EpCAMlo cells were shown to have significantly increased migratory and invasive ability when compared with their EpCAMhi counterparts (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by invasion assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A.

claim: EpCAMlo cells have significantly reduced EPCAM mRNA expression compared to EpCAMhi cells.
source: Significantly reduced mRNA levels of EPCAM and E-cadherin (CDH1), and increased expression of vimentin (VIM) and of the EMT-transcription factor ZEB1 were observed in EpCAMlo cells from both lines, as also confirmed by immunofluorescence (IF) analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: EpCAMlo cells have significantly reduced CDH1 (E-cadherin) mRNA expression compared to EpCAMhi cells.
source: Significantly reduced mRNA levels of EPCAM and E-cadherin (CDH1), and increased expression of vimentin (VIM) and of the EMT-transcription factor ZEB1 were observed in EpCAMlo cells from both lines, as also confirmed by immunofluorescence (IF) analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: EpCAMlo cells have significantly increased VIM (vimentin) mRNA expression compared to EpCAMhi cells.
source: Significantly reduced mRNA levels of EPCAM and E-cadherin (CDH1), and increased expression of vimentin (VIM) and of the EMT-transcription factor ZEB1 were observed in EpCAMlo cells from both lines, as also confirmed by immunofluorescence (IF) analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: EpCAMlo cells have significantly increased ZEB1 mRNA expression compared to EpCAMhi cells.
source: Significantly reduced mRNA levels of EPCAM and E-cadherin (CDH1), and increased expression of vimentin (VIM) and of the EMT-transcription factor ZEB1 were observed in EpCAMlo cells from both lines, as also confirmed by immunofluorescence (IF) analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B and immunofluorescence in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D.

claim: Knockdown of ZEB1 expression by shRNA dramatically decreases the percentage of EpCAMlo cells in HCT116 and SW480 cell lines.
source: Accordingly, knockdown of ZEB1 expression by shRNA dramatically decreased the percentage of EpCAMlo cells in both lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B-C after ZEB1 knockdown.

claim: All five members of the miR-200 family show significantly reduced expression in EpCAMlo cells compared to EpCAMhi cells.
source: RT-qPCR analysis of sorted cells revealed significantly reduced expression levels of all five miR-200 members in EpCAMlo cells from both cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), that is, in agreement with the observed increase in ZEB1 expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: EpCAMlo cells show decreased mitotic activity compared to EpCAMhi cells.
source: Proliferation and cell cycle analysis indicated decreased mitotic activity in EpCAMlo cells from both cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E,F and Figure 1—source data 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by proliferation assay and cell cycle analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3E,F.

claim: EpCAMlo cells show increased viability at all tested oxaliplatin concentrations compared to EpCAMhi and bulk cells.
source: EpCAMlo cells showed increased viability at all tested oxaliplatin (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,C, left panels) and 5-FU (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,D, left panels) concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by MTT viability assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,C.

claim: EpCAMlo cells show increased viability at all tested 5-FU concentrations compared to EpCAMhi and bulk cells.
source: EpCAMlo cells showed increased viability at all tested oxaliplatin (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A,C, left panels) and 5-FU (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,D, left panels) concentrations.
evidence: The claim is supported by MTT viability assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B,D.

claim: EpCAMlo cells from both HCT116 and SW480 are able to re-enter the cell cycle at a broad range of oxaliplatin and 5-FU concentrations when compared with EpCAMhi cells.
source: Likewise, regrowth assays revealed that EpCAMlo cells from both cell lines are able to re-enter the cell cycle at a broad range of oxaliplatin and 5-FU concentrations when compared with EpCAMhi cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4, right panels).
evidence: The claim is supported by regrowth assay data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 right panels.

claim: Liver metastases from EpCAMlo cells show heterogeneous β-catenin localization with membranous and cytoplasmic localization in the center and nuclear accumulation in the periphery.
source: Notably, immunohistochemistry (IHC) analysis of the resulting liver metastases revealed a heterogeneous pattern of intracellular β-catenin, with membranous and cytoplasmic localization in cells from within the center of the lesion, and nuclear β-catenin accumulation in cells localized in the periphery, thus recapitulating what is observed in primary colon carcinomas (Fodde and Brabletz, 2007; Kirchner and Brabletz, 2000; Figure 1—figure supplement 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5A and cited references.

claim: Doxycycline induction of Zeb1 expression in AKP organoids increases EpCAMlo cells from 4.8% to 22-76% in primary tumors.
source: FACS analysis of the primary tumor revealed an increase in EpCAMlo cells from 4.8% in the non-induced tumors up to 22–76% upon dox-induction of Zeb1 expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5D.

claim: Continuous doxycycline administration in AKP-Z transplanted mice results in only a marginal increase of lung and liver metastases compared to control animals.
source: As expected, only a marginal increase of lung and liver metastases was observed in AKP-Z transplanted mice upon continuous dox administration in the drinking water for 8 weeks when compared with control (no dox) animals (Figure 1—figure supplement 5E), likely to result from the continuous induction of Zeb1 expression and the consequent inhibition of METs essential for metastasis formation (Brabletz et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by metastasis quantification data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5E and cited reference.

claim: The majority of EpCAMlo cells from HCT116 and SW480 revert to the epithelial EpCAMhi phenotype when cultured under conventional conditions.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, while the majority of EpCAMlo cells from both cell lines revert to the epithelial phenotype, only a minority of EpCAMhi cells switches to the more mesenchymal state.
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis over time shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Only a minority of EpCAMhi cells switch to the EpCAMlo mesenchymal state when cultured under conventional conditions.
source: As shown in Figure 2A, while the majority of EpCAMlo cells from both cell lines revert to the epithelial phenotype, only a minority of EpCAMhi cells switches to the more mesenchymal state.
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis over time shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Late EpCAMlo cells show significantly increased CDH1 and EPCAM expression compared to early EpCAMlo cells.
source: Accordingly, CDH1 and EPCAM expression was significantly increased in 'late' (e.g., cultured for >60 and >100 days, respectively) vs. 'early' EpCAMlo cells (e.g., collected after <7 days of culture), whereas VIM and ZEB1 expression was decreased in 'late' vs. 'early' EpCAMlo cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Late EpCAMlo cells show decreased VIM and ZEB1 expression compared to early EpCAMlo cells.
source: Accordingly, CDH1 and EPCAM expression was significantly increased in 'late' (e.g., cultured for >60 and >100 days, respectively) vs. 'early' EpCAMlo cells (e.g., collected after <7 days of culture), whereas VIM and ZEB1 expression was decreased in 'late' vs. 'early' EpCAMlo cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The migratory capacity of late EpCAMlo HCT116 cells is reduced to levels comparable with those of early EpCAMhi cells.
source: In addition, the migratory capacity of 'late' EpCAMlo HCT116 cells was reduced to levels comparable with those of 'early' EpCAMhi cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by transwell migration assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The majority of EpCAMlo single cells are capable of generating substantial percentages of EpCAMhi progeny to recapitulate the heterogeneous composition of the parental cell lines.
source: As shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1, the majority of EpCAMlo single cells were capable of generating substantial percentages of EpCAMhi progeny to eventually recapitulate the heterogeneous composition of the parental cell lines (e.g., Figure 2B, clones 2F12 and 2E10).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell clonogenicity assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: A minority of EpCAMlo single cells lose plasticity and retain the EpCAMlo phenotype even after extended culture.
source: A minority of the cells, however, appears to have lost this plasticity and retains, even after extended culture, the EpCAMlo phenotype (e.g., Figure 2B, clone 2H12).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell clonogenicity assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The majority of EpCAMhi single cells retain their epithelial features with <1% switching to the EpCAMlo state.
source: In contrast, the majority of EpCAMhi single cells retained their epithelial features with <1% switching to the EpCAMlo state (Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell clonogenicity assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: EpCAMlo cells have slightly increased doubling times compared to EpCAMhi cells in HCT116 (1.09 vs. 1.00 days).
source: First, the FACS data was employed to estimate the average doubling time of cells in both populations; slightly increased doubling times were reported for EpCAMlo compared to EpCAMhi cells in both lines (HCT116: 1.09 vs. 1.00 days; SW480: 1.86 vs. 1.68 days).
evidence: The claim is supported by Markov model analysis of FACS data.

claim: EpCAMlo cells have slightly increased doubling times compared to EpCAMhi cells in SW480 (1.86 vs. 1.68 days).
source: First, the FACS data was employed to estimate the average doubling time of cells in both populations; slightly increased doubling times were reported for EpCAMlo compared to EpCAMhi cells in both lines (HCT116: 1.09 vs. 1.00 days; SW480: 1.86 vs. 1.68 days).
evidence: The claim is supported by Markov model analysis of FACS data.

claim: EpCAMlo cells show a higher transition probability to EpCAMhi compared to the reverse transition (8.1-fold in HCT116 and 4.0-fold in SW480).
source: Of note, EpCAMlo cells show a higher transition probability compared to EpCAMhi (8.1- and 4.0-fold in HCT116 and SW480, respectively) (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Markov model fitting shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Subclones with lower plasticity gain dominance within a few months in culture.
source: We ran a simulation of this effect by starting from a culture with multiple subclones having distinct transition probabilities; the results indicate that subclones with lower plasticity gain dominance within a few months (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by simulation data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: RNAseq analysis identified 152 differentially regulated genes between EpCAMhi and EpCAMlo cells in HCT116.
source: A total of 152 and 353 differentially regulated genes were identified between the EpCAMhi and EpCAMlo cells in HCT116 and SW480, respectively (p. adjusted<0.01, when applying a log2 fold change <–1.5 and > 1.5).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq differential expression analysis.

claim: RNAseq analysis identified 353 differentially regulated genes between EpCAMhi and EpCAMlo cells in SW480.
source: A total of 152 and 353 differentially regulated genes were identified between the EpCAMhi and EpCAMlo cells in HCT116 and SW480, respectively (p. adjusted<0.01, when applying a log2 fold change <–1.5 and > 1.5).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAseq differential expression analysis.

claim: Only 34 differentially regulated genes are common between HCT116 and SW480 EpCAMlo cells.
source: Among these, only a relatively few (n = 34) were common to both lines (Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of RNAseq differential expression results.

claim: IPA of combined EpCAMlo expression profiles shows significant associations with EMT regulation, Wnt/β-catenin signaling, human ESC pluripotency, IL8 signaling, and colorectal cancer metastasis.
source: Nonetheless, IPA of the combined EpCAMlo expression profiles highlighted significant associations with EMT regulation, Wnt/β-catenin signaling, human ESC pluripotency, IL8 signaling, and colorectal cancer metastasis (Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ingenuity Pathway Analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Treatment with 4 µM Chiron (GSK3β inhibitor) results in robust Wnt signaling activation in HCT116 and SW480 cell lines.
source: Indeed, upon treatment with the glycogen synthase 3β (GSK3β) inhibitor CHIR99021 (Chiron), a robust Wnt signaling activation was observed in both cell lines by TopFLASH reporter assay (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by TOP-Flash luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Chiron treatment leads to an approximately threefold increase of the EpCAMlo population in HCT116 cells.
source: FACS analysis of the treated cell lines showed that the enhancement of Wnt signaling led to an approximately threefold increase of the EpCAMlo population in the HCT116 cell line, though not in SW480 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Chiron treatment does not increase the EpCAMlo population in SW480 cells.
source: FACS analysis of the treated cell lines showed that the enhancement of Wnt signaling led to an approximately threefold increase of the EpCAMlo population in the HCT116 cell line, though not in SW480 (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Chiron treatment is consistently accompanied by an increase in ZEB1 expression in both HCT116 and SW480 cell lines.
source: However, IF analysis showed that Chiron treatment was consistently accompanied by an increase in ZEB1 expression in both cell lines, in agreement with the role of ZEB1 as a downstream Wnt target (Sánchez-Tilló et al., 2011; Sánchez-Tilló et al., 2015; Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3E and cited references.

claim: Isogenic HCT116 cell lines show a progressive increase in EpCAMlo subpopulation from 3.9% in HCT116-WT to 7.9% in HCT116-P and 28.7% in HCT116-MT cells.
source: FACS analysis of these cell lines revealed a progressive increase in the EpCAMlo subpopulation from 3.9% in HCT116-WT to 7.9% in HCT116-P and 28.7% in HCT116-MT cells (Figure 3F).
evidence: The claim is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Co-localization of nuclear β-catenin and ZEB1 expression was found in 5 out of 25 colon carcinoma cases investigated at the invasive front.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, co-localization of nuclear β-catenin and ZEB1 expression was found in 5 out of 25 cases investigated.
evidence: The claim is supported by IHC analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Expression of HCT116 and SW480 EpCAMlo signatures is highly correlated with each other in the CMS3232 human colon cancer cohort.
source: Expression of the HCT116 and SW480 signatures was highly correlated with each other (Figure 4A), with the CMS4 signature genes (n = 143) (Figure 4A–B), and with the expression signature of colon cancer cell lines previously classified as mesenchymal-like (CCS3) (De Sousa et al., 2013; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Expression of HCT116 and SW480 EpCAMlo signatures is highly correlated with the CMS4 signature genes in the CMS3232 human colon cancer cohort.
source: Expression of the HCT116 and SW480 signatures was highly correlated with each other (Figure 4A), with the CMS4 signature genes (n = 143) (Figure 4A–B), and with the expression signature of colon cancer cell lines previously classified as mesenchymal-like (CCS3) (De Sousa et al., 2013; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A-B.

claim: Expression of HCT116 and SW480 EpCAMlo signatures is highly correlated with the CCS3 mesenchymal-like colon cancer cell line signature.
source: Expression of the HCT116 and SW480 signatures was highly correlated with each other (Figure 4A), with the CMS4 signature genes (n = 143) (Figure 4A–B), and with the expression signature of colon cancer cell lines previously classified as mesenchymal-like (CCS3) (De Sousa et al., 2013; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and cited reference.

claim: High expression of EpCAMlo signatures from both HCT116 and SW480 identifies a group of primary colon cancer patients with significantly shorter overall survival.
source: High expression of the EpCAMlo signatures from both cell lines identifies a group of primary colon cancer patients with a high propensity to form metastases and with significantly shorter overall survival (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: High expression of EpCAMlo signatures identifies a group of primary colon cancer patients with a high propensity to form metastases.
source: High expression of the EpCAMlo signatures from both cell lines identifies a group of primary colon cancer patients with a high propensity to form metastases and with significantly shorter overall survival (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Single-cell RNA sequencing analyzed more than 1000 cells from each EpCAMlo and EpCAMhi subpopulation.
source: More than 1000 cells were analyzed from each subpopulation and sequenced to a depth of approximately 50,000 reads each with the MiSeq System (Illumina).
evidence: The claim is stated in the methods description for scRNAseq.

claim: EpCAMlo and EpCAMhi cells from HCT116 cluster in separate groups after tSNE dimension reduction.
source: After dimension reduction with tSNE, the EpCAMlo and EpCAMhi cells clustered in separate groups in HCT116 (Figure 5A), whereas the SW480 cells showed a partial overlap between the two subpopulations and a distinct EpCAMhi cluster, identified as the non-adherent subpopulation within the SW480 cell line ('spheres') (Hirsch et al., 2014; Yi et al., 2020; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by tSNE analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: SW480 cells show a partial overlap between EpCAMlo and EpCAMhi subpopulations and a distinct EpCAMhi cluster identified as the non-adherent 'spheres' subpopulation.
source: After dimension reduction with tSNE, the EpCAMlo and EpCAMhi cells clustered in separate groups in HCT116 (Figure 5A), whereas the SW480 cells showed a partial overlap between the two subpopulations and a distinct EpCAMhi cluster, identified as the non-adherent subpopulation within the SW480 cell line ('spheres') (Hirsch et al., 2014; Yi et al., 2020; Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by tSNE analysis shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, and cited references.

claim: Using an EMT signature for dimension reduction clearly resolves EpCAMlo and EpCAMhi subpopulations in both HCT116 and SW480.
source: Using this 'EMT signature,' the two subpopulations were clearly resolved both in HCT116 and SW480 (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by supervised tSNE analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: HCT116 shows a clear transition from EpCAMhi to EpCAMlo with a minority of 'in-between' cells earmarked by high pEMT scores.
source: While HCT116 showed a clear transition from EpCAMhi to EpCAMlo with a minority of 'in-between' cells earmarked by high pEMT scores, in SW480 the transition appeared to be accompanied by higher levels of intercellular variance.
evidence: The claim is supported by EMT score analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: In SW480, the transition from EpCAMhi to EpCAMlo is accompanied by higher levels of intercellular variance.
source: While HCT116 showed a clear transition from EpCAMhi to EpCAMlo with a minority of 'in-between' cells earmarked by high pEMT scores, in SW480 the transition appeared to be accompanied by higher levels of intercellular variance.
evidence: The claim is supported by EMT score analysis of scRNAseq data.

claim: EPCAM and CDH1 expression gradually decreases over the EMT axis in scRNAseq analysis.
source: As expected, epithelial expression of EPCAM and CDH1 gradually decreased over the EMT axis, while mesenchymal genes such as ZEB1 and VIM, and Wnt target genes such as AXIN2 and DKK1, showed opposing behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression trend analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: ZEB1 and VIM expression increases over the EMT axis in scRNAseq analysis.
source: As expected, epithelial expression of EPCAM and CDH1 gradually decreased over the EMT axis, while mesenchymal genes such as ZEB1 and VIM, and Wnt target genes such as AXIN2 and DKK1, showed opposing behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression trend analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Wnt target genes AXIN2 and DKK1 expression increases over the EMT axis in scRNAseq analysis.
source: As expected, epithelial expression of EPCAM and CDH1 gradually decreased over the EMT axis, while mesenchymal genes such as ZEB1 and VIM, and Wnt target genes such as AXIN2 and DKK1, showed opposing behavior.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene expression trend analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Wnt signaling level increases over the EMT axis in scRNAseq analysis.
source: More generically, the level of Wnt signaling ('Wnt.score'), measured by the activation of the WNT_PATHWAY from the PID database, increased over the EMT axis (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Wnt score analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: SPARC expression peaks at intermediate EMT states, indicative of a partial EMT state.
source: We evaluated the expression trends of other genes upregulated in EpCAMlo cells and observed that SPARC (osteonectin) peaked in between the extremities of the EMT axis, indicative of a partial EMT state (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPARC expression trend analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: RNA velocity analysis shows that the majority of cells are moving in their respective state, with both EpCAMlo and EpCAMhi states including source and sink points.
source: Consistent with the fitted Markov model, the majority of cells were moving in their respective state, and both states included source and sink points that could elicit or inhibit plasticity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: On a population level, EpCAMlo cells are more likely to transit to EpCAMhi cells than vice versa according to PAGA analysis.
source: On a population level, EpCAMlo cells were more likely to transit to EpCAMhi cells than vice versa (by partition-based graph abstraction or PAGA; Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by PAGA velocity graph shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Only a small population of cells is captured in the process of transitioning between EpCAMlo and EpCAMhi identities.
source: In fact, only a small population of cells was captured in the process of transitioning to the other identity (Figure 5E).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The plastic population of transitioning cells shows the highest pEMT score.
source: This apparently plastic population, earmarked by the opposing velocity arrows, showed the highest pEMT score (Figure 5F), as well as high SPARC expression (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by pEMT score projection shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The plastic population of transitioning cells shows high SPARC expression.
source: This apparently plastic population, earmarked by the opposing velocity arrows, showed the highest pEMT score (Figure 5F), as well as high SPARC expression (Figure 5G).
evidence: The claim is supported by SPARC expression projection shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Unsupervised clustering of HCT116 scRNAseq data reveals 8 distinct subclusters: three of EpCAMhi origin and five EpCAMlo.
source: Unsupervised clustering using shared neighbor (SSN) modularity optimization revealed the presence of distinct subclusters (n = 8): three of EpCAMhi origin and five EpCAMlo (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by unsupervised clustering shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Cluster analysis reveals four sets of EMT signature genes expressed in different combinations throughout the different clusters.
source: This analysis revealed four sets of genes expressed in different combinations throughout the different clusters.
evidence: The claim is supported by k-means clustering of EMT signature genes shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Gene set mes1, including ZEB1, VIM, and SNAI2, is expressed throughout the EpCAMlo clusters.
source: Notably, gene set mes1, including ZEB1, VIM, and SNAI2, is expressed throughout the EpCAMlo clusters, while gene set mes2, including SPARC, FN1, and TWIST1, is mostly expressed in the pEMT EpCAMlo cluster (#7).
evidence: The claim is supported by cluster analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Gene set mes2, including SPARC, FN1, and TWIST1, is mostly expressed in the pEMT EpCAMlo cluster (#7).
source: Notably, gene set mes1, including ZEB1, VIM, and SNAI2, is expressed throughout the EpCAMlo clusters, while gene set mes2, including SPARC, FN1, and TWIST1, is mostly expressed in the pEMT EpCAMlo cluster (#7).
evidence: The claim is supported by cluster analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Partial EMT clusters #6 and #7 show distinct expression of gene sets indicating alternative activation of specific arrays through which partial EMT cells arise.
source: Of note, the partial EMT clusters #6 and #7 showed distinct expression of these gene sets indicating alternative activation of specific arrays through which partial EMT cells arise (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by cluster analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E-F.

claim: Overexpression of SPARC in HCT116 and SW480 results in a marked increase in the expression of EMT-TFs ZEB1 and SNAI2.
source: As SPARC earmarks pEMT states (Figure 5D), we overexpressed it in the HCT116 and SW480 cell lines and observed a marked increase in the expression of EMT-TFs (ZEB1 and SNAI2) and the corresponding up- and downregulation of mesenchymal and epithelial markers in EpCAMlo cells and a corresponding increase in their motility and invasive capacity (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Overexpression of SPARC results in up- and downregulation of mesenchymal and epithelial markers in EpCAMlo cells.
source: As SPARC earmarks pEMT states (Figure 5D), we overexpressed it in the HCT116 and SW480 cell lines and observed a marked increase in the expression of EMT-TFs (ZEB1 and SNAI2) and the corresponding up- and downregulation of mesenchymal and epithelial markers in EpCAMlo cells and a corresponding increase in their motility and invasive capacity (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR analysis shown in Figure 5H.

claim: Overexpression of SPARC results in a corresponding increase in motility and invasive capacity of EpCAMlo cells.
source: As SPARC earmarks pEMT states (Figure 5D), we overexpressed it in the HCT116 and SW480 cell lines and observed a marked increase in the expression of EMT-TFs (ZEB1 and SNAI2) and the corresponding up- and downregulation of mesenchymal and epithelial markers in EpCAMlo cells and a corresponding increase in their motility and invasive capacity (Figure 5H).
evidence: The claim is supported by migration assay data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The CMS4_RF signature shows the highest association with normal and tumor stromal cells in scRNAseq data from Lee et al., 2020.
source: Based on the latter study, as depicted in Figure 6A, the CMS4_RF signature shows the highest association with normal and tumor stromal cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of scRNAseq data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The CMS4_RF signature is clearly enriched among CMS4 tumors in the bulk RNAseq cohort of 3232 patients.
source: At the bulk RNAseq level, using the larger (n = 3232 patients) cohort of colon tumors from Guinney et al., 2015, the CMS4_RF signature is clearly enriched among the CMS4 tumors (Figure 6B) and is likewise associated with poor survival (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by bulk RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The CMS4_RF signature is associated with poor survival in colon cancer patients.
source: At the bulk RNAseq level, using the larger (n = 3232 patients) cohort of colon tumors from Guinney et al., 2015, the CMS4_RF signature is clearly enriched among the CMS4 tumors (Figure 6B) and is likewise associated with poor survival (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The CMS4_TC signature shows the highest association with epithelial tumor cells in scRNAseq data.
source: Accordingly, the CMS4_TC signature shows the highest association with epithelial tumor cells (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The CMS4_TC signature shows increased association with both CMS1 and CMS4 tumors at the bulk RNA level.
source: Of note, at the bulk RNA level, the CMS4_TC signature shows increased association with both CMS1 and CMS4 tumors (Figure 6E) and outperforms the CMS4_RF signature in stratifying patients on survival (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by bulk RNAseq analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The CMS4_TC signature outperforms the CMS4_RF signature in stratifying patients on survival.
source: Of note, at the bulk RNA level, the CMS4_TC signature shows increased association with both CMS1 and CMS4 tumors (Figure 6E) and outperforms the CMS4_RF signature in stratifying patients on survival (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The CMS4_TC signature can stratify patients from CMS1 and CMS3 groups on survival.
source: The same CMS4_TC signature can clearly stratify patients from CMS groups other than CMS4, and in particular CMS1 and CMS3, on survival (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mesenchymal-like tumor cells represent 9.7% of all tumor cells in the scRNAseq data from Lee et al., 2020.
source: In order to identify EpCAMlo cells in primary colorectal tumors, we took advantage of the scRNAseq data from Lee et al., 2020 to annotate the tumor cells with highest association to the CMS4_TC signature as mesenchymal-like (Mes-like = 9.7% of all tumor cells).
evidence: The claim is supported by annotation of scRNAseq data from Lee et al., 2020.

claim: Tumor cells from CMS1 and CMS4 patients show the highest association to the CMS4_TC signature.
source: In agreement with the observations made at the bulk RNA level, tumor cells from CMS1 and CMS4 patients showed the highest association to the CMS4_TC signature (Figure 6G).
evidence: The claim is supported by scRNAseq analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Mesenchymal-like tumor cells show lower expression of EPCAM compared to bulk tumor cells.
source: Differential expression between the mesenchymal-like and bulk tumor cells revealed lower expression of EPCAM, while higher expression of CD44 and mesenchymal markers such as VIM, COL1A1, MMP7, ECM1, and SPARC (Figure 6H), the latter previously identified to peak at intermediate EMT levels and predicted by RNAvelocity to earmark a subpopulation of plastic cells transitioning in between states (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: Mesenchymal-like tumor cells show higher expression of CD44, VIM, COL1A1, MMP7, ECM1, and SPARC compared to bulk tumor cells.
source: Differential expression between the mesenchymal-like and bulk tumor cells revealed lower expression of EPCAM, while higher expression of CD44 and mesenchymal markers such as VIM, COL1A1, MMP7, ECM1, and SPARC (Figure 6H), the latter previously identified to peak at intermediate EMT levels and predicted by RNAvelocity to earmark a subpopulation of plastic cells transitioning in between states (Figure 5D–G).
evidence: The claim is supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 6H.

claim: HCT116 is representative of the microsatellite instability (MIN) colon cancer subtype.
source: Here, we mainly focused on the HCT116 and SW480 lines as they are representative of the two main colon cancer subtypes earmarked by microsatellite instability (MIN) and chromosomal instability (CIN; also known as microsatellite stable [MSS]), respectively (Lengauer et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited reference.

claim: SW480 is representative of the chromosomal instability (CIN/MSS) colon cancer subtype.
source: Here, we mainly focused on the HCT116 and SW480 lines as they are representative of the two main colon cancer subtypes earmarked by microsatellite instability (MIN) and chromosomal instability (CIN; also known as microsatellite stable [MSS]), respectively (Lengauer et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited reference.

claim: The adenoma-carcinoma sequence in colon cancer is characterized by a stepwise buildup of genetic alterations in specific oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes.
source: This is exemplarily illustrated by the adenoma-carcinoma sequence in colon cancer where a stepwise buildup of genetic alterations in specific oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes underlies tumor initiation and progression (Fearon and Vogelstein, 1990).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited reference.

claim: Epigenetic changes, rather than genetic mutations, underlie phenotypic plasticity in cancer.
source: However, with regard to the capacity to disseminate through the tumor microenvironment and establish metastases in distant organ sites, epigenetic changes, rather than genetic mutations, underlie what is the most clinically relevant hallmark of cancer, namely phenotypic plasticity (Varga and Greten, 2017; Teeuwssen and Fodde, 2019).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited references.

claim: EMT bestows cancer cells with stem-like plastic characteristics needed to acquire quasi-mesenchymal features at the invasive front.
source: EMT bestows cancer cells with stem-like plastic characteristics (Mani et al., 2008) needed to acquire quasi-mesenchymal features at the invasive front of the primary tumor, disseminate and attain therapy resistance, and to revert back to more epithelial states (mesenchymal to epithelial transition [MET]) at the organ site of metastasis (Brabletz et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited references.

claim: Epigenetic activation and silencing of EMT-inducing transcription factors underlies the transient nature of cellular modifications during EMT.
source: Epigenetic activation and silencing of EMT-inducing transcription factors (EMT-TFs) underlies the transient nature of these cellular modifications (Skrypek et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited reference.

claim: The 'migrating cancer stem cell' (mCSC) model was first proposed for colon cancer by T. Brabletz.
source: The 'migrating cancer stem cell' (mCSC) model has been first proposed for colon cancer by T. Brabletz (Brabletz et al., 2005), also as a solution to the so-called 'β-catenin paradox' (Fodde and Brabletz, 2007).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited references.

claim: In the majority of sporadic colorectal cancer cases, loss of the APC tumor suppressor is predicted to lead to nuclear β-catenin translocation and full-blown Wnt signaling activation.
source: In the majority of sporadic colorectal cancer cases, the rate-limiting loss of the APC tumor suppressor is predicted to lead to nuclear β-catenin translocation and full-blown Wnt signaling activation.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents established knowledge.

claim: Tumor cells with nuclear β-catenin represent only a small minority of the primary lesion and tend to cluster at the invasive front of colon carcinomas.
source: Notwithstanding these predictions, tumor cells with nuclear β-catenin represent only a small minority of the primary lesion and tend to cluster non-randomly at the invasive front of colon carcinomas where they gain mesenchymal features to detach and disseminate into the adjacent stromal tissues.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents an observation.

claim: Cues secreted from the tumor microenvironment elicit EMT downstream of full-blown Wnt signaling activation in cells at the invasive front of colon carcinomas.
source: In view of these observations, it is plausible that cues secreted from the tumor microenvironment elicit EMT downstream of full-blown Wnt signaling activation, earmarked by nuclear β-catenin, in a subset of cells located at the invasive front (Brabletz et al., 2005; Fodde and Brabletz, 2007).
evidence: The claim is stated as a plausible hypothesis supported by cited references.

claim: Human immortalized breast cancer cell lines encompass different subpopulations of cells with distinct phenotypic states maintained in a dynamic equilibrium through stochastic transitions.
source: Previously, it was shown that human immortalized breast cancer cell lines encompass different subpopulations of cells with distinct phenotypic states and functional characteristics maintained in a dynamic equilibrium through stochastic transitions between states (Gupta et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited reference.

claim: In oral squamous carcinoma cell lines, non-EMT CSCs are proliferative and retain epithelial characteristics, while EMT-competent CSCs are quasi-mesenchymal with increased cellular motility.
source: Similar observations were made in oral squamous carcinoma cell lines where distinct CSC phenotypes are present: whereas non-EMT CSCs are proliferative and retain epithelial characteristics, the EMT-competent CSC fraction is (quasi)mesenchymal and of increased cellular motility (Biddle et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited reference.

claim: The mesenchymal CMS4 subtype accounts for approximately 25% of colon cancer cases and is associated with the greatest propensity to form metastases.
source: The mesenchymal CMS4 subtype accounts for approximately 25% of the cases and is associated with the greatest propensity to form metastases.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents established knowledge from CMS classification.

claim: Bona fide tumor cells from stroma-rich cancers have a markedly mesenchymal gene expression pattern.
source: While the CMS4 signature was initially attributed to the presence of tumor-associated stroma and not to a cancer cell-intrinsic property (Calon et al., 2015; Isella et al., 2015), it has been shown that bona fide tumor cells from stroma-rich cancers have a markedly mesenchymal gene expression pattern (Vellinga et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited references.

claim: Hybrid E/M or partial EMT cells are thought to be endowed with increased invasive and metastatic capacity.
source: Recent studies on the role of EMT in eliciting phenotypic plasticity in cancer cells have highlighted the relevance of intermediate cellular stages co-expressing both epithelial and mesenchymal genes for tumor progression and metastasis (Jolly et al., 2015; Aiello et al., 2018; Pastushenko et al., 2018). These hybrid E/M or partial EMT cells are thought to be endowed with increased invasive and metastatic capacity.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited references.

claim: SPARC is a matricellular protein involved in the modulation of cell-cell and cell-matrix interactions and is known as a prognostic marker in colon cancer.
source: Partial EMT cells, predicted by RNAvelocity to transit between states, are characterized not only by the co-expression of E- and M-specific genes at intermediate levels, but also by increased expression of specific genes like SPARC (Secreted Protein Acidic and Rich in Cysteine, also known as osteonectin), encoding for a matricellular protein involved in the modulation of cell–cell and cell–matrix interactions and known as a prognostic marker in colon cancer (Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited reference.

claim: SPARC triggers EMT through direct cell-to-cell contact and upregulation of other EMT-inducers like fibronectin (FN1).
source: Importantly, SPARC triggers EMT through direct cell-to-cell contact and upregulation of other EMT-inducers like fibronectin (FN1) (Takigawa et al., 2017), reminiscent of the interactions occurring between parenchymal and stromal cells at the invasive front in colon cancer (Fodde and Brabletz, 2007) where pEMT is expected to underlie plasticity and invasion through the ECM.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited references.

claim: CTCs with less pronounced epithelial characteristics are likely to underlie metastasis at distant organ sites.
source: Although current detection methodologies mainly rely on their epithelial features, more recent studies have indicated that CTCs with less pronounced epithelial characteristics are likely to underlie metastasis at distant organ sites.
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and represents recent findings.

claim: In breast and oral cancer, hybrid E/M tumor cells feature the highest degree of phenotypic plasticity coupling the capacity of undergoing EMT/MET with therapy resistance and other stem cell features.
source: In breast and oral cancer, hybrid E/M tumor cells feature the highest degree of phenotypic plasticity coupling the capacity of undergoing EMT/MET with therapy resistance and other stem cells features (Yu et al., 2013; Biddle et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is stated in the text and supported by cited references.
